articles.title: Some critical questions
articles.content: TRUE to tradition, a ‘plan’ to ‘reset’ the country’s entire structure has come down like an epiphany from apparently ‘non-political’ quarters. The plan envisages creating multiple provinces and changing the country’s very tapestry — its geography, topography, demography, ethnic relations, resource distribution, power sharing, and broader political calculus. The situation raises critical questions. Why new provinces? The interior minister, whoannounced the plan, hasn’t held forth on the reasoning or offered an acceptable justification for adopting such an extreme and hazardous course. However, he has mentioned bad governance, population implosion, and systemic failures as some of the causes. Nor are there any official authoritative studies proposing a close nexus between good governance and smaller administrative structures. In fact, the global landscape reveals a mixed pattern. Some countries have fewer or territorially larger constituent units, and yet they are stable, functional, even enviable. Others have multiple small units/ provinces, but are perennially afflicted with broken, inept and even failed political systems. The factors that generally determine the performance and vitality of a state are the legitimacy and efficacy of its political system, the character and ability of its leadership, and the maturity and capacity of its institutions — not only to deliver better governance, but also to meet the continuing challenges thrown up by ever-changing societal and state imperatives. In revitalising the ‘failed’ political systems, we don’t know if the so-called plan contemplates these factors. Who is demanding them? Interestingly, most of these ideas have originated outside regular political processes, whether as One Unit, Basic Democracy, ‘Islamisation’, enlightened moderation, or hybrid governance. People have always been on the receiving end of new-fangled ideas and their pernicious consequences. The call for a structural ‘reset’, too, appears to have similar origins. So far, none of the governments — federal, provincial or even local — or the mainstream political leaderships have called for restructuring the provinces. However, there is near-consensus across the political spectrum on creating provinces in south Punjab, and KP’s Hazara belt. In fact, the Punjab and KP assemblies passed resolutions for these provinces, but they went nowhere. Instead of new units, the country needs softer options to heal societal wounds. Reorganising the state structures would be an extremely risky exercise. India’s Congress party had included the ‘linguistic’ provinces in its manifesto as early as 1917. Yet, after Partition, both prime minister Jawaharlal Nehru and home minister Vallabhbhai Patel were reluctant to reorganise the states, fearing balkanisation of the fledgling country. It was many months of intense political agitations across the country, expert studies, judicial commissions, and a much-mourned fast unto death by Telugu nationalist Potti Sriramulu that finally brought the government around. Still, the Reorganisation Act of 1955 was not passed to improve governance but to group various linguistic communities in their own separate states. In other words, distinctive ethno-cultural identities were recognised and restored, rather than brutally denied and suppressed as would have been the case if the states had been broken up in a manner that dispersed the historically located ethno-cultural communities — something that is being contemplated here. Is referendum feasible? Perhaps encouraged by the smooth passage of the controversial26thand27thconstitutional amendments, and not expecting a large section of the political establishment to oppose the proposed move, some elements here had appeared confident of securing the required numbers to ensure restructuring. However, the JUI-F, ANP, PTI, and even the ruling party’s major coalition partner have dug in their heels. In fact,even the prime minister and his partyseem reluctant to support the restructuring, though some government ministers are backing it, albeit without the cabinet’s approval. Likewise, the Sindh Assembly has alsorejectedthe break-up of the province. As a result, other means are being sought — preferably, a referendum to execute the plan. But a referendum would not validate the wholesale reorganisation of the state. It lacks legitimacy and credibility. It cannot be used to circumvent or be a substitute for the mandatory constitutional amendment. People will not accept it because every military dictator has used it to legitimise their rule. Instead, a referendum will be seen as farcical and incite public anger, triggering a maelstrom of pushback. Will the ‘plan’ succeed? Any idea, policy, or law that is imposed on the people has miserably failed to achieve its objectives; in fact, it has often led to disasters. Steamrolling the restructuring of provinces — against the will of the people — will further aggravate identity-driven politics across a fragile multiethnic landscape. It may even ignite the tinderbox the country has become, particularly for poor and disgruntled youth who have endured the harrowing realities of failed systems. The numbers are dreadful. Half the population lives in poverty, around 28 million children are out of school, four out of 10 children suffer from stunted growth, three-fourths of the populace is consuming contaminated water, and the increasingly murky security environment scares away local and foreign investors. In these dire circumstances, the country desperately needs softer options to heal societal wounds — options that recompense the people through justice, equity, peace, opportunity, and development, which are democracy’s tested tools. The yawning fault lines — ethnic, social, political, inter-provincial and centre-province — must be mended, and federal democracy, which remains buried under the hybrid regime, restored. The system does need a ‘reset’. But the reset should mean building efficient and accountable institutions, strengthening rules-based governance, and allowing legitimate and representative leadership to run political and public offices. That requires a continuous process of fair, free elections held on time, so that dead wood can be replaced with a fresher, cleaner leadership at the federal, provincial, and local levels. Finally, a ‘reset’ would be fatal if it ignored the emotional, even spiritual, bonding of the various ethno-cultural communities with their respective provinces. This bonding goes beyond ideology or politics. It is the product of the centuries-long interplay between these communities and their distinctive land, history, culture, language, literature and art. This bonding leads many in Sindh to conceive their province as an indivisible historical entity — a firmer federalised version of Scotland or Quebec.
articles.author: Shahab Usto

articles.title: Iran’s emergence
articles.content: AN especially dangerous moment is opening up as the war in the Middle East transitions gears. The warlaunchedby Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu back in February has effectively ended. It devolved into a stand-off around Hormuz. What is opening up now is something new. And where this takes us is the big unknown. A big power is emerging to our west. Shackled by sanctions for decades, and threatened incessantly with war, Iran had been walled away from the rest of the world since 1979. But now that America has demonstrated its impotence by failing every military objective it had laid in the war since February, the country that was tied down behind a wall of sanctions is emerging as a big power in the region. In that sense, what is happening with Iran today is similar to what happened with China following détente. That country, too, was tied down and shackled and shunned by the global community ever since its revolution in 1949. Détente was its negotiated re-entry into the community of nations, and since then, the reforms undertaken within China propelled it to becoming a global power. Iran’s story differs from this in the sense that it is not going to be a global power. However, it is certainly going to emerge as a regional power in a very important region of the world. Second, Iran’s re-entry into the world community is going to be far more disorderly than that of China, mainly because it has had to fight its way out of the oblivion into which it was banished since the revolution of 1979. Short of an attempt to destroy its infrastructure, Iran’s emergence as a big power in the region is unstoppable. But emergence is now underway. It will be a very disorderly, and possibly violent, affair. A lot depends on which faction within Iran manages to rise to the top and take over decision-making. In China, an internal reckoning took place within the Communist Party first, before the reform-minded elements around Deng Xiaoping could rise to the top and take control of the post-opening up trajectory. That is a fraught history, from the Cultural Revolution and the purge of Deng in 1966, to the attempted coup by Lin Biao and his death in a plane crash in Mongolia in 1971, to the rise of Zhou Enlai and the so-called Gang of Four that was ranged against him and the eventual emergence of Deng as the successor, his second purge after Zhou Enlai’s death, and eventual restoration following Mao’s death in 1976. That is when China firmly embarked on its reformist course and broke its moorings to Mao’s thought. What followed was a carefully calibrated set of measures designed to open the Chinese economy up to the outside world — slowly and experimentally. That trajectory eventually propelled China towards becoming a global power, even if the process took many decades to complete. Iran is now at a similar point in its trajectory. Following thedeath of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, and its victory in the war against the Zionist alliance of America and Israel, it now has to go through the internal process of wrangling between rival factions, who must decide whether to remain wedded to the past or break out into a new future. This process will take years to unfold; what makes the Iranian trajectory different from the Chinese one is that in Iran the process will unfold in the context of a war. It is evident that within Iran there is a pragmatic faction that wants to see the war come to a close and the task of rebuilding the country to begin. But equally important, there is a faction that wants to press ahead with the fighting to deliver a humiliating defeat to the aggressors. This faction wants to do to the Americans in the Middle East what the Taliban, too, did to them in Afghanistan:force a hurried and disorderly flight from the region. The real game begins after that. Once the Americans leave the region, the Iranian military machine will turn its attention towards the Gulf monarchs. There will be reparations to pay. The bill for the war has already been served. In July 2025, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told theFinancial Timesthat there could be no return to nuclear talks until Iran had been compensated for the damage caused by the June war. America scoffed at the demand. In March 2026, the demand was made again in the counter-offer that Iran made to the American proposal for talks. In April, they added an amount — $270 billion — while another figure of $300bn was written into theUS-Iran MOU in June 2026. Nobody should be scoffing at the demand now. In addition to retaining control of Hormuz, Iran will press this demand in the days to come and it is the Gulf monarchs who will be left to pay the bill once the US decides the conflict no longer serves any of its interests. And once the Gulf monarchs settle this amount, another will surface. And then another. Iran’s emergence as a big power in the region is now unstoppable, short of an attempted catastrophic destruction of the entire country’s infrastructure by the Zionist alliance. This may be an unlikely outcome at this point in time, but it cannot be ruled out. The emergence as a big power is already underway. After consolidating their control on Hormuz, they will next turn their gaze to the riches of the Gulf monarchs. Those riches are now imperilled. China’s story is instructive here because it tells us that a post-revolutionary polity can manage its affairs to secure its re-entry into the global system of trade, finance and diplomacy to procure maximum benefits for itself. Whether Iran manages this moment similarly, or whether they decide to press their military advantage to the hilt and use their newfound centrality to avenge the past rather than build a future, is the big question hanging over all of us today. The writer is a business and economy journalist.
articles.author: Khurram Husain

articles.title: Royal baubles
articles.content: GLITTERING baubles of gold and oversize jewels distinguish royalty from commoners. Had the Egyptian pharaoh Tutankhamun been buried without his regalia, he would have been just another anonymous handful of dust. He was a minor pharaoh compared to his wealthier predecessors. Their richer tombs were systematically denuded by brazen grave-robbers. Descendants of the Aztec empire might still have the fabled treasures of their ancestors, had the greedy Spanish conquistadors not invaded and ravished Latin America in 1519-20. Countless Chinese imperial treasures were destroyed by Anglo-French invaders during the Second Opium War in 1860, when they ransacked the Old Summer Palace in Beijing. Anything precious that remained of China’s cultural heritage was smuggled out to Taiwan by Gen Chiang Kai-shek in 1949-50. The magnificent jewels looted by Nadir Shah when he drained the imperial Mughal treasury in 1739 are stored today in the Bank Melli in Tehran. They underpin Iran’s currency. Post-Revolution Russians since 1922 have stored their imperial treasures in the Kremlin. The British Crown jewels would have been wealthier had Oliver Cromwell not melted and sold some of them during the brief period of Britain’s other commonwealth (1653-58). Modern rulers prefer to keep their tangible assets in real estate or tax-proof havens. Only royalty flaunts its higher status with bejewelled crowns and tiaras. Royalty watchers are intrigued by the speed with which the present Queen Camilla is using the royal baubles left by her in-laws. One cache of Crown property was inherited by King Charles as monarch from his ancestress Queen Victoria. These include the Kohinoor and the Lahore Durbar diamonds and emeralds (purloined from the Sikhs), and gifts from obsequious maharajas. Another glittering hoard came from Charles’s great-grandmother — the acquisitive Queen Mary. Her appetite for jewellery was insatiable. When the Romanovs fled Russia in 1918 and were forced to sell their jewels, she bought the now famous Vladimir tiara from the Grand Duchess Marie Feodorovna in 1921, and a spectacular cabochon sapphire and diamond brooch from the exiled Empress Marie Feodorovna’s collection. Queen Mary lived long enough to bequeath these and other heirlooms directly to her granddaughter — the regnant Queen Elizabeth II. She skipped the less favourite Queen Elizabeth (later the Queen Mother). Only royalty flaunts its higher status with crowns and tiaras. A third group of jewellery came to King Charles from the bequest of Queen Alexandra. She died in 1925 and left some important jewels to the “future wife” of her grandson Edward (then Prince of Wales). His subsequent marriage to Mrs Wallis Simpson caused heartburn within the royal family. Many tactless attempts were made by Lord Mountbatten to wrest the jewellery from her. These are finally in Charles’s possession. A fourth important group has a decidedly plebeian origin. In 1942, Dame Margaret Greville — believed to be the illegitimate daughter of a Scottish brewer from his cook — sent a tin trunk containing priceless jewellery to her friend Queen Elizabeth (later the Queen Mother). Despite the obvious defect in her pedigree, Dame Margaret had insinuated herself into royal circles. She hosted Elizabeth and her groom Albert (later George VI) during their honeymoon. Although she knew Queen Mary, she bypassed the greedy dowager and gave her collection instead to the daughter-in-law. In 1942, during the war, Queen Elizabeth, on opening the shimmering contents of the mundane trunk, wrote to Queen Mary: “I must tell you that Mrs Greville has left me her jewels, tho’ I am keeping THAT quiet for the moment!” She wore those jewels sparingly in public, perhaps to avoid criticism from nascent republicans, and her envious in-laws. She displayed them fully only in the late 1950s after Queen Mary’s death. Prominent amongst them is a monumental diamond tiara commissioned by Dame Margaret from Boucheron in Paris in 1921. Matching it is a spectacular five-row festoon necklace, bought from Cartier. It sparkles with diamonds and emeralds set in platinum. Both have become a part of Queen Camilla’s regalia. Another Greville gift — a pair of diamond chandelier earrings — is worn often by Catherine Princess of Wales. In 2023, at their coronation, King Charles and Queen Camilla, in deference to Charles’s down-scaled ‘green’ monarchy, required all female royals to wear “embroidered floral headpieces instead of diamonds”. Diamonds may be forever, but on this occasion, they were kept beyond their reach. Queen Camilla, however, a spry 80-year old, has exempted herself from her own rules. She appears determined to enjoy every carat in the royal vaults. A republican Cockney landlady once dismissed such overladen royals with the jibe: “If you were to smother me with diamonds, I too would look like them!”
articles.author: F.S. Aijazuddin

articles.title: Ties with UAE
articles.content: PAKISTAN-UAE relations have stood the test of time despite geopolitical upheavals. The current souring of relations does not reflect the true potential of ties between the two countries. Bilateral ties are rooted in shared faith, cultural affinity, and enduring people-to-people bonds. Pakistan was among the first countries to recognise and establish diplomatic relations with the UAE after the country’s founding in 1971. Since then, ties have continued to expand. Pakistan’s contribution to the UAE’s development remains an important glue that still binds the two states together. Pakistani military personnel, engineers, teachers, professionals and skilled workers have contributed to defence, aviation, education, and engineering. A 2.2 million-strong Pakistani diaspora remains an important pillar of the UAE economy, contributing $8 billion in remittances, while also providing demographic balance vis-à-vis 4.2m Indian expatriates. The UAE is Pakistan’s third-largest trading partner. There is steady progress towards investment-led partnerships in logistics, technology, agriculture and food security. This is supported by the Pakistan-UAE Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, which is expected to raise trade volume to $16-20bn. Pakistan’s 240m consumer market, young, tech-savvy workforce, 2.3m freelancers, and 26,000 registered IT/ITeS companies offer significant opportunities for UAE investment in Pakistan’s IT parks, fintech, and e-commerce. Pakistan’s defence ties with the UAE date back to 1974, when 115 Pakistani defence personnel laid the foundations of an enduring partnership by training Emirati pilots and military personnel, and establishing the Armour Training School. The extent of cooperation is evident in the fact that the first five chiefs of air staff of the UAE Air Force were Pakistan Air Force officers. Pakistan offers joint special forces training exercises for counterterrorism and co-production of defence hardware, on account of its advanced defence industry, along with prospects for future cooperation in AI, cyberspace, electronic warfare, and advanced defence systems. Ties between Pakistan and the UAE have continued to expand. Agriculture and food security is another area of convergence due to Pakistan’s fertile land and the UAE’s demand for agricultural products. Pakistan’s climatic conditions, agricultural workforce and production capacity can contribute to UAE food security. Conversely, UAE capital, technology, and logistics can make Pakistan’s supply chains more resilient through cold-chain storage, marketing, and value addition. Minerals are another area of cooperation. Pakistan possesses immense mineral wealth. Already, Pakistan’s Mari Energies is collaborating with the UAE’s International Resource Holding to explore copper and gold reserves in Chagai, as well as opportunities in antimony, aluminium ore, and rare earth elements. A few UAE companies are also exploring the possibility of establishing an ore-refining industry in Punjab. Geopolitical challenges like the UAE’s joining of the Abraham Accords and its economic rivalry with Saudi Arabia have resulted in political cleavages that have widened during the Iran-US conflict. Israel’s expansionist policies have not helped; the UAE’s quest for regional peace has foundered on the rocks of Israeli militarism. The UAE’s policies in Somaliland, Algeria, Libya, Yemen and Sudan have often placed it in Saudi Arabia’s rival camp. Israel and the UAE are increasingly collaborating in some fields, and India’s influence is also growing because of its close ties with the former. However, Pakistan understands each country’s choices and does not have a direct clash of interest with any of the I2U2 (India, Israel, the USA, UAE) states. Pakistan wants to play the role of regional stabiliser in West Asia through alliances like the Makkah defence alliance. Pakistan’s mediatory role in the Iran-US conflict has also created space for the UAE’s rapprochement with Iran. Pakistan and the UAE face a common threat in transnational terrorism and organised crime. As a global trade and transshipment hub, the UAE faces direct threats from the narco-trade emanating from Afghanistan. Pakistan’s ports like Karachi, Port Qasim and Gwadar complement rather than compete with UAE ports, lessening their burden and relieving congestion in Hormuz. The scope for counterterrorism cooperation is broad. The two can combine Pakistan’s CT intelligence experience with the UAE’s capabilities in financial monitoring, border and aviation security, cybersecurity, etc to disrupt threats. Pakistan and the UAE should take advantage of the full range of economic, defence and CT cooperation opportunities, since their common interests far outweigh any geopolitical differences.
articles.author: Dr Raashid Wali Janjua

articles.title: Managing the shock
articles.content: THE energy shock Pakistan faces calls for immediate demand management.Houthi attackson Saudi energy infrastructure and shipping have strained an already fragile supply chain by disrupting oil and gas flows through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Global oil prices have been pushed to their highest level since May. A net energy importer, Pakistan has felt the impact directly:petrol has risento Rs384.34 per litre and high-speed diesel to Rs415.83. Pain at the pump is pushing people to the edge. Moreover, higher global oil prices are feeding into the import bill, transport costs and inflation, adding further pressure on financially strained families. RLNG prices have also risen. The government says greater use of domestic energy sources has helped keep power plants running. Domestic resources accounted for 72pc of electricity generation in August. Without more domestic gas for power generation, we could have faced another hour of loadshedding and an additional Rs10.6bn in consumer tariffs. That may provide some respite but is not a reason for complacency. Energy conservation must start now. That does not mean shutting the country down. A nationwide lockdown would cost businesses working hours, deplete workers’ income, and hit daily-wage earners hard — a burden that an economy already struggling to generate growth and jobs cannot easily absorb. What the government should pursue, instead — at least for now — is targeted conservation: measures that cut avoidable consumption without halting productive activity. Schools could shorten operating days to ease transport and electricity demand. Government offices and private employers can be encouraged to work from home where practical. Markets, especially in major cities, could close earlier to cut late-night transport and commercial power use. Malls, offices and commercial buildings should face reasonable limits on unnecessary lighting and cooling. Government departments need to lead by example rather than leave conservation to households alone. Provinces must follow suit so that the effort is not fragmented. The prime minister’sfuel relief packagefor motorcycle and small car owners may cushion a small part of the population, but subsidies cannot fix a supply shock, and protecting fuel consumption through the budget only gets costlier as global prices climb. The priority now is to protect incomes and essential economic activity while cutting non-essential demand. The larger point is that Pakistan cannot keep meeting every external energy shock by either subsidising the cost or shutting down activity. Building domestic solar energy availability, grid efficiency, storage capacity and public transport is what actually reduces this vulnerability over time. Meanwhile, the choice is not between business as usual and a lockdown. There is a lot of room between the two. And the government needs to use it: conserve early, cut waste, keep the economy running.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Bab al-Mandeb closure
articles.content: AS the pro-Iran Houthis battle both the Saudis and the Riyadh-backed Yemeni government, alarm bells are ringing across the world over the economic shockwave the long-term closure of the Bab al-Mandeb strait would send across the globe. The militia, which controls significant territory in Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, has, over the past few days of fighting, consolidated its gains around the strait. The Houthis say that passage through the channel is open for all except Saudi vessels — against whom they have vowed to enforce a “blockade for blockade”. Yet this will do little to reassure crews, as few vessels will want to pass through an active war zone. The Strait of Hormuz — that other major regional chokepoint — is already practically closed due to the US war on Iran. If shipping traffic through Bab al-Mandeb also grinds to a halt, the global economy will be in very dangerous territory. The government has said Pakistan faces an energy crunch. But Pakistan is not alone; disruption in the strait or the Red Sea will have an impact far and wide. Protests have been reported from as far afield as Syria and Indonesia, and if the situation worsens, more public unrest is likely as fuel pumps run dry. Therefore, the Houthis — whatever their differences with the Saudis or the Yemeni government — must reconsider closure of Bab al-Mandeb, and pledge to keep it open for all vessels. As the Pakistani representative told the UN Security Council the other day, any attempt to “threaten, obstruct, or weaponise” vital waterways will have negative effects on international trade and shipping, as well as energy security. He added that “diplomacy must assume urgency”. The need for talks cannot be emphasised enough. The region cannot afford more violence; the Yemeni people have already suffered for over a decade, while the global economy is on tenterhooks due to the situation in Yemen. As the Saudis have enforced a blockade of Houthi-held territory since 2015, Riyadh could offer to lift the blockade if the militia stopped their attacks on the kingdom’s territory. Furthermore, a Yemeni-led, Yemeni-owned peace process is essential domestically. All belligerents need to step back and give talks a chance, as an escalation in violence would be catastrophic for the region.
articles.author: Editorial
